stimulus.text:
| Group | Response to the Declaration |
| African Americans | Its natural-rights language seemed to challenge slavery. Jefferson's first draft blamed slavery on Britain, but Congress removed that passage. Some enslaved people fled to the British; some in the North won freedom by serving in the militia or the Continental Army. |
| Native Americans | Most supported the British, fearing the land hunger of the new nation. |
| Women | Revolutionary ideals inspired the idea of republican motherhood: women would educate their sons to be citizens of the republic, so mothers themselves needed education. |

books.section: B. Common Sense, the Declaration of Independence, and Republican Self-Government

stem: Congress voted for independence on July 2, 1776, and the Declaration was announced on July 4. What does this dating most clearly show?

options.text: That the Declaration was written in a single day
options.misconception: The draft was written in June by Jefferson and his committee — the dates show a vote and an announcement, not a day of writing.

options.text: That Congress was divided and nearly rejected independence
options.misconception: Background: the vote on July 2 was not unanimous at first, but the dating itself shows a decision followed by an announcement, not a near-rejection.

options.text: That July 4 marks the day the war with Britain began
options.misconception: The war had begun more than a year earlier, at Lexington and Concord in April 1775.

options.text: That July 4 marks the announcement of a decision Congress already made

rationales.D: Congress voted for independence on July 2; July 4 is the day the decision was announced to the world. The holiday honors the telling, not the deciding.
rationales.A: Jefferson drafted the Declaration in June. The July dates mark the vote and the announcement, not the writing.
rationales.B: The dating shows a vote followed by an announcement. It does not by itself show a near-rejection.
rationales.C: Fighting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775, more than a year before July 1776.
rationales.general:
1. Separate the two dates. July 2 is the vote for independence; July 4 is the announcement.
2. Ask what July 4 therefore marks. Not the decision itself, but the day it was told to the world.
3. Name the distinction. A decision and its announcement are two events, and the holiday honors the second.
Remember: dates that sit two days apart usually mark two different acts — voting and announcing are not the same thing.
